narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were, in order: your LSAT score, your class ranking after the third year of law school, and your undergraduate GPA. 

Your LSAT score of 38 was the strongest influence, and it worked in your favor by pushing the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was outweighed by the other two features. Your third-year class ranking of 4 was noticeably lower than the average ranking of about 5.8 among students who were accepted, and this pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. Similarly, your undergraduate GPA of 2.7 sits well below the 3.23 average of accepted students and added further weight toward a likely bar exam failure.

Taken together, these academic performance signals led the model to conclude that the risk of failure was too high for admission. 

To improve your chances next time, focus on raising your class rank through stronger performance in later law school years and consider retaking the LSAT if possible. These two areas appear to be the biggest levers for changing the outcome. (218 words)
